abstract: Global networks of public crop breeding programs exchange germplasm to share traits and increase diversity for genetic gain. There is a fundamental dilemma in crop breeding between the need to expand the genetic variation in elite gene pools while avoiding disruptions to essential traits required for eliteness. One particular challenge in admixed germplasm is the release of undesired transgressive segregation due to the disruption of favorable epistatic haplotypes of essential traits, which may stymie deployment of genomic selection (GS) In this study, we used breeding simulations to model recurrent population improvement for an annual crop species that can be selfed and crossed to examine the effectiveness of GS in admixed germplasm. We quantified the genetic heterogeneity between founder lines with an isoeliteness score, an effect size-weighted Hamming distance using quantitative trait loci markers. Populations with low founder isoeliteness (i.e. low genetic compatibility) had lower genetic gain with GS in early cycles than those with high founder isoeliteness (63% and 27% lower after 2 and 4 cycles). To mitigate this, we developed an isoeliteness-guided GS (isoGS) method to recover favorable epistatic haplotypes in a segregating population, which enabled 31% and 15% more genetic gain after 4 and 20 cycles. Our results suggest that founder isoeliteness scores and isoGS are valuable tools for overcoming the diversity vs. eliteness dilemma by managing the introduction of genetic diversity in a trait-specific manner.
